title: Floods: what is standing fact
summary: India has counted flood damage every year since 1953, and the count is a compilation of what states chose to report. Two official series exist, built from different state returns under different definitions, and in recent years they differ by a factor of three.
india_relevance: Flooding is the most consequential hazard on this page and the least well counted. The Central Water Commission compiles state returns; the National Crime Records Bureau compiles police returns; neither measures anything directly, and for 2022 one recorded 1,673 flood deaths where the other recorded 547. The figure most often quoted for India's flood-prone area — 40 million hectares — is a 1980 estimate that CWC's own satellite work has since roughly halved.

figures.label: Average annual flood deaths
figures.note: The base period is load-bearing: the same series gives 1,670 on a 1953–2022 base and 1,710 on 1953–2023. The long average is also dominated by pre-1980 years — 11,305 people died in 1977 alone.

figures.label: The same year, counted twice
figures.note: CWC's compilation against NCRB's. The gap is structural, not an error: CWC compiles state disaster returns for 'floods and heavy rains'; NCRB compiles police records for the narrower cause 'flood'. Adding NCRB's landslide and torrential-rain deaths still only reaches 905. Neither series is a subset of the other.

figures.label: Average annual damage, cost-indexed
figures.note: CWC's own inflation-adjusted figure. The nominal average for the same period is ₹7,267 crore — comparing 1970s rupees with 2020s rupees without this adjustment is meaningless, and most citations do exactly that.

figures.label: Flood-prone area, measured by satellite
figures.note: CWC's 2024 assessment on Landsat and Sentinel imagery, 1986–2022. The ubiquitous '40 million hectares' is a 1980 Rashtriya Barh Ayog estimate derived from 1953–1978 data by assuming the worst year's damage was the area at risk. NRSC's 2023 atlas gives 15.75 million ha.

figures.label: Worst year on record for damage
figures.note: Against records of 17.52 million ha affected in 1978 and 70.46 million people affected in the same year.

figures.label: CWC flood forecasting stations
figures.note: 53 of them in the North-East. The same reply notes that the number of embankment failures and breaches is not maintained centrally at all.

figures.label: Share of flood-affected area in the Ganga basin
figures.note: About 15% is Brahmaputra and 30–35% the rest. Aggregated flood-affected area 1986–2022: Uttar Pradesh 5.17 million ha, Bihar 2.91, Assam 2.48, West Bengal 1.84.

precedents.what: The reporting basis changed. From this year CWC's column counts deaths AND missing persons on the wider MHA 'floods and heavy rains' definition, and moves bridge, dam and road damage outside the headline total — so 2023 and 2024 cannot be compared with earlier years.

toll.label: deaths and missing — not comparable with 2022's 1,673

precedents.what: The Yamuna reached 208.66 m at Delhi's Old Railway Bridge, passing the 207.49 m of September 1978 — the highest level ever recorded there.
precedents.card: Yamuna at Delhi, highest ever recorded

precedents.what: The deadliest flood year in the seventy-two-year record, and the reason the long-run average sits near 1,700 deaths a year.
precedents.card: The deadliest flood year on record

not_counted: Whatever a state chose not to report. For 2024 Assam filed 'Not Reported' against crop value, house value, public utilities and total damage — while reporting 1.39 million ha affected and 110 deaths. A dozen other states did the same, so the published national total is a floor, not an estimate.
Embankment failures and breaches. A 2025 parliamentary answer states this is not maintained centrally at all.

Infrastructure, in the headline figure. From 2023 damage to bridges, dams, roads and irrigation sits outside the published total — in 2024 that excluded ₹10,447 crore, more than the entire reported total.
Urban flooding as a distinct category. There is no national dataset separating it from riverine flooding.

sources.title: Statistics of Flood Damage Data for India, 1953–2024, Annexure-II
sources.note: CWC compiles rather than measures: the data are state returns confirmed against the Home Ministry's disaster-management portal. Figures are silently revised between editions — 2022's total damage reads ₹27,392 crore in one publication and ₹27,337 crore in another.

sources.title: Report on Flood Damage Statistics 1953–2022, Publication CWC/2024/120
sources.note: Its overview states plainly that the data are as furnished by the states and that gaps remain for 2021 and 2022.

sources.title: Accidental Deaths & Suicides in India 2022, chapter 1
sources.note: NCRB states in terms that the data come from state police and that it is not responsible for their authenticity. 2022 is the latest edition carrying this series; 2023 and 2024 flood figures are not published.

sources.title: Assessment of Areas Affected due to Floods in India, 2024 — satellite assessment 1986–2022
sources.note: Link is to Part II, which is confirmed live. The earlier estimates it supersedes are the Rashtriya Barh Ayog's 40 million ha (1980) and a 2011 working group's 49.8 million ha.

withheld: '40 million hectares of India is flood-prone' — a 1980 estimate from 1953–1978 data, derived by treating the worst single year's damage as the area at risk. CWC's own 2024 satellite assessment gives 21.2 million ha and NRSC's 15.75 million ha.
Any bare 'average flood deaths per year' without its base period — the same official series yields 1,670, 1,708 or 1,710 depending on whether it ends in 2022, 2023 or 2024.

'India lost 113,943 lives and US$53 billion to floods, 1953–2017' — CWC publishes rupees only, and warns that the nominal series needs cost-indexing before any comparison across decades. No dollar total is a CWC output.
2023's death figure read as a year-on-year rise. It is the first year on a wider definition that also counts missing persons; the apparent jump is a change of basis, not a change in the weather.

causes.label: Extreme rainfall
causes.short: Rain over the catchment beyond what the channel and the drains can carry.
causes.evidence: India Meteorological Department daily rainfall for the district against its own heavy (64.5 mm) and very heavy (115.5 mm) day categories.

causes.label: Reservoir or barrage release
causes.short: Water released from storage upstream, on top of the rain.
causes.evidence: The operator's own gate-operation log and the Central Water Commission's downstream gauge record for the same hours.

causes.label: Embankment or drain failure
causes.short: A bund, embankment or stormwater drain giving way rather than overtopping.
causes.evidence: A state irrigation department breach report, which names the location and the length.

causes.label: Drainage that could not carry it
causes.short: Built surface and blocked channels turning ordinary rain into a flood.
causes.evidence: Whether the same streets flood at the same rainfall every year, which is a records question rather than a hydrology one.

what_to_watch: River levels at the Central Water Commission's gauges downstream, and whether any cross a warning or danger mark.
Whether more rain is forecast over the same catchment before the water has gone down.
Whether any upstream reservoir is near capacity, since a release adds to a river that is already high.
Embankments already under strain, where a breach moves the flood somewhere new rather than deeper.
The casualty and displacement figures settling. Early counts move for a week and different agencies count the displaced differently.
what_later: Waterborne disease in the weeks after the water goes down, which is counted separately from the flood and often not attributed to it.
Crop loss that only becomes a figure at harvest, months later.
Silt in the channel changing where the next flood goes.
Displacement that does not reverse, which no published series tracks.
_precedent_card: A SHORT CARD TITLE, AUTHORED. It used to be taken as the first sentence of `what`, which works for 'South Lhonak Lake, Sikkim. 14.7 million...' and fails twice over: for 'Chorabari Lake above Kedarnath, Uttarakhand, overtopped its moraine and...' the first full stop is 100 characters in, so the card printed its own date twice; and flood.json's precedents are milestones in a record rather than events at a place, so no slice of them is a place at all. The prose stays in `what` and is shown in full in the disclosure below the cards.
